sections.overview: The Senegal galago, also called the northern lesser galago or Senegal bushbaby, is a small strepsirrhine primate in the family Galagidae. Despite its name, it ranges far beyond Senegal across sub-Saharan Africa, from western regions toward the Horn and East Africa. Four subspecies are commonly recognised, though boundaries and some taxonomy remain under study. It is a nocturnal, tree-living primate, but regularly descends to the ground.
sections.identification: The body averages about 13 cm long; the consulted species account gives 95–300 g as the mass range for the genus, not a species-specific estimate. No dependable adult sex-specific measurements or body width were found, so those values are not inferred. This galago has a compact body, soft grey to brown fur, a pale stripe down the nose, very large mobile ears, and forward-facing eyes that reflect torchlight. A reflective layer behind the retina returns some incoming light through the photoreceptors, improving the chance of detecting photons in dim conditions; it does not create light. Long fingers and toes end in broadened, grippy pads for holding branches. A comb of lower front teeth and a narrow grooming claw on the second toe of each hind foot help maintain the coat.
sections.habitat: Across its broad range, the species uses woodland, bushland, savanna and some montane habitats rather than one uniform forest type. Local observations illustrate this flexibility: the Senegal subspecies occurs in open Acacia–baobab woodland in The Gambia, while populations elsewhere use moist woodland, riverine forest and wooded grassland. In northern Tanzania, researchers found sleeping sites with dense canopy and connected neighboring trees. Such cover can hide a resting animal from aerial predators, while connected branches provide escape routes; cooler, more humid sleeping locations also support a thermoregulatory explanation. These results describe one Tanzanian site and season, not every population.
sections.diet: The Senegal galago eats arthropods and tree exudates such as gum. At a northern Tanzanian site, researchers directly observed both foods but did not collect enough data to estimate their dietary proportions. During a separate dry-season study at Fongoli in southeastern Senegal, they did not see fruit eating; fruit has been recorded in The Gambia. These observations suggest local and seasonal flexibility, not one universal menu. Gum is an energy-rich plant secretion, often released after insect damage to bark, and gives the galago a food source distinct from mobile insect prey.
sections.behavior: The galago’s night is divided between travel, feeding, pauses and self-maintenance. Powerful hind limbs and elongated ankle and foot bones help it cling upright to a trunk, then launch into a leap; elastic tendons and connective tissues store energy during crouching and release it rapidly at take-off. This spring-like mechanism amplifies muscle power, while the long tail helps stabilize the body in motion. Grooming combines licking and combing with the lower toothcomb and hind-foot grooming claw. Social life is neither strictly solitary nor continuously group-based: individuals often forage alone, but may sleep together and keep contact by calls. A Tanzanian study found social patterns differed substantially among sites.
sections.reproduction: Females bear dependent young that require milk, warmth and protection while their coordination develops. A mother may carry an infant in her mouth or let it cling to her fur, and may leave it concealed while she forages. A 1960 study of the nominate subspecies in Sudan described oestrous cycles lasting four to six weeks throughout the year, with a local peak of sexual activity in mid-December in the Nuba Mountains. This did not establish a fixed breeding season across the species. Maternal care is central; reproductive timing and male involvement remain less well documented across populations.
sections.ecology: By eating arthropods, galagos are predators of small invertebrates, although their effect on prey populations has not been quantified well enough to claim broad ecosystem control. They also exploit gums produced when insects damage Acacia trees, linking the primate’s feeding to a plant’s response to injury and to the insects beneath the bark. A striking predator–prey interaction was documented at Fongoli, Senegal: chimpanzees sometimes probe tree cavities with sharpened sticks to capture sleeping galagos. This is a local hunting technique, not a general account of chimpanzee diets or of galago mortality across Africa.
sections.conservation: The IUCN’s global assessment conducted in 2016 and published in 2019 classified Galago senegalensis as Least Concern, consistent with its extensive range. This category is a global risk assessment, not proof that every local population is stable or that habitat change is harmless. Nocturnal galagos are difficult to detect, and information remains sparse for many populations, making local abundance hard to establish. Woodland conversion and degradation can remove sleeping cover and feeding trees locally; the degree of risk depends on the site. The category alone does not establish the condition of any particular population.
